subject: phy
title: Waves
subtitle: Wave properties, types, speed and the electromagnetic spectrum.
concept: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter; transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to propagation, longitudinal waves have oscillations parallel.
Wave speed v = fλ; the frequency of a wave is determined by its source, while wavelength changes when speed changes (e.g. refraction).
The electromagnetic spectrum spans radio waves to gamma rays; all travel at 3×10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum.

notes.heading: Wave Properties
items: Period (T): time for one complete oscillation; T = 1/f.
Wavelength (λ): distance between two successive in-phase points (e.g. crest to crest).
Phase difference: measured in degrees or radians; two points λ apart are in phase (0° or 2π); λ/2 apart are antiphase (180° or π).

notes.heading: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
items: Transverse: oscillations ⊥ to propagation direction; e.g. EM waves, water waves, S-waves (seismic).
Longitudinal: oscillations ∥ to propagation direction; compressions and rarefactions; e.g. sound, P-waves (seismic).
Polarisation: only transverse waves can be polarised; oscillations restricted to one plane.

notes.heading: Reflection, Refraction, Diffraction
items: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from normal).
Refraction: wave changes speed (and wavelength) at a boundary; frequency stays constant; n = c/v = sin θ₁/sin θ₂ (Snell's law).
Total internal reflection: occurs when angle of incidence ≥ critical angle (sin c = 1/n). Used in optical fibres.
Diffraction: spreading of waves around obstacles or through gaps; most significant when gap ≈ λ.

notes.heading: Electromagnetic Spectrum
items: Order (increasing frequency/decreasing wavelength): radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma.
All EM waves: transverse; travel at c = 3×10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum; can be polarised.

Uses: radio (broadcasting), microwave (communications, cooking), IR (thermal imaging), visible (sight), UV (fluorescence, sterilisation), X-rays (medical imaging), gamma (cancer treatment, sterilisation).

definitions.body: The distance between two successive points that are in phase (e.g. crest to crest); symbol λ; unit: metre.
The restriction of transverse wave oscillations to a single plane; only transverse waves can be polarised.
The angle of incidence at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary (angle of refraction = 90°); beyond this angle, total internal reflection occurs.
The spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle; most pronounced when the gap width ≈ wavelength.

workedExamples.q: Light travels from glass (n = 1.5) to air. Find the critical angle.
A sound wave of frequency 440 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹. Find its wavelength.

mistakes: Confusing frequency (stays constant at a boundary) with wavelength (changes at a boundary during refraction).
Applying polarisation to longitudinal waves — only transverse waves can be polarised.
Using the wrong formula for critical angle: sin c = 1/n (only when going from medium of refractive index n to air/vacuum).
tips: At a refractive boundary: f = constant; v and λ both change. Remember 'frequency is fixed by the source'.
Polarisation evidence for transverse nature: if a wave can be polarised → must be transverse.
Diffraction: wider gap → less diffraction. Wavelength closer to gap size → more diffraction.

flashcards.q: What is the critical angle and when does total internal reflection occur?
flashcards.a: Critical angle c: sin c = 1/n. TIR occurs when angle of incidence ≥ c (light going from denser to less dense medium).

flashcards.q: What quantity stays constant when a wave refracts at a boundary?
flashcards.a: Frequency stays constant; speed and wavelength both change.

flashcards.q: Why can only transverse waves be polarised?
flashcards.a: Polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane. Longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel to propagation — there is only one direction, so no polarisation is possible.

flashcards.q: State the order of the electromagnetic spectrum from lowest to highest frequency.
flashcards.a: Radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma ray.
When the gap width is approximately equal to the wavelength of the wave.

questions.q: A wave has frequency 200 Hz and wavelength 1.5 m. What is its speed?

questions.exp: Sound is a longitudinal wave — oscillations are parallel to propagation direction; polarisation is only possible for transverse waves.

questions.q: Light enters a medium and slows down. What happens to its wavelength?
questions.exp: v = fλ; frequency is constant; if v decreases, λ must also decrease proportionally.

questions.q: What is the condition for total internal reflection?
opts: Angle of incidence = angle of refraction
Angle of incidence ≥ critical angle, going from denser to less dense medium
questions.exp: TIR occurs when light hits a boundary (from denser to less dense medium) at an angle ≥ the critical angle.

questions.q: Which part of the EM spectrum has the shortest wavelength?
questions.exp: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength in the EM spectrum.

recall: State and apply the wave equation.
Describe transverse and longitudinal waves with examples.
Explain what happens to frequency, wavelength and speed at a refractive boundary.
Derive the formula for critical angle and calculate it.
Explain why polarisation is evidence that light is a transverse wave.
